title: InSight: Battle with Dust
subtitle: Keep a solar-powered seismometer alive on Mars while dust slowly buries its panels.
intro: 26 NOV 2018 — 19:52:59 UTC. Touchdown confirmed in Elysium Planitia, Mars.
InSight carries SEIS, a seismometer that will listen to the interior of Mars.
It has no nuclear battery and no brushes for its panels. Every watt comes from the Sun.
Your job: make the decisions that keep it listening for as long as possible.

events.title: Power on the surface
events.text: InSight has survived entry, descent and landing, but it is running on its battery. The two round solar arrays are still folded. The dust kicked up by landing is still settling.

choices.label: Deploy both solar arrays now, on landing day
choices.outcome: The arrays fan open within hours of landing and start recharging the batteries. At first they produce around 5,000 watt-hours per sol.

source.label: NASA JPL — InSight Is Catching Rays on Mars

choices.label: Wait a few sols for landing dust to settle
choices.outcome: The battery keeps draining while the arrays stay closed. You open them just in time, but the batteries took a deep discharge.

fact.title: Why you should not wait
fact.text: A lander arrives with only the energy stored in its batteries. InSight deployed its arrays on landing day so it could recharge immediately; delaying would mean deep battery discharge and colder electronics.

source.label: NASA JPL — InSight Is Catching Rays on Mars

events.discuss: Why does a solar-powered lander open its panels as soon as possible after landing? What would you check first?

events.title: Where should the seismometer live?
events.text: SEIS is still sitting on the lander deck. The robotic arm can lift it and place it on the ground — something no spacecraft has done on another planet before.

choices.label: Lift SEIS with the arm and set it on the Martian ground
choices.outcome: On 19 December 2018 InSight placed its seismometer on Mars — the first time a seismometer was robotically placed on another planet. A wind and thermal shield later covered it.

source.label: NASA JPL — NASA’s InSight Places First Instrument on Mars

choices.label: Leave it on the deck — less risk for the arm
choices.outcome: The seismometer records mostly the lander itself: wind shaking the deck and panels. The data are noisy.

fact.title: Why not to measure from the deck
fact.text: A seismometer must touch the ground to feel quakes travelling through the planet. InSight’s plan was to place SEIS directly on the surface with its arm and then cover it with a wind and thermal shield.

source.label: NASA JPL — NASA’s InSight Places First Instrument on Mars

events.discuss: Why is a seismometer more useful on the ground than on the lander deck? Think about wind and vibration.

events.title: The mole will not dig
events.text: The heat probe, nicknamed the “mole”, is meant to hammer itself several metres down. Since 28 February 2019 it keeps bouncing in place. The soil clumps instead of flowing around the probe.

choices.label: Use the arm’s scoop to press on and pin the mole for friction
choices.outcome: Pinning helps: the mole gets 2–3 cm below the surface. But after 500 more hammer strokes on 9 January 2021 with no progress, the team ends the effort. The arm learned skills it was never designed for — they will matter later.

source.label: NASA — NASA InSight’s ‘Mole’ Ends Its Journey on Mars

choices.label: Keep hammering at full power until it breaks through
choices.outcome: Thousands of strokes later the mole is still bouncing in its pit. You burned energy and stressed the mechanism.

fact.title: Why hammering alone fails
fact.text: The mole needed friction from the soil to balance the recoil of its hammer. Mars’ soil at the site clumped and gave too little friction, so the probe bounced in place. Extra hammering cannot create friction.

source.label: NASA — NASA InSight’s ‘Mole’ Ends Its Journey on Mars

events.discuss: Engineers tested many fixes for the mole. When should a team decide to stop trying?

events.title: The panels are getting dusty
events.text: Dust settles on the arrays every sol. Spirit and Opportunity were sometimes cleaned by passing whirlwinds. InSight has detected many whirlwinds — none have cleaned it. The team needs an idea.

choices.label: Pulse the array deployment motors to shake the dust off
choices.outcome: It was worth a try. The motors last used when the panels opened are pulsed — but the dust does not come off. The team keeps thinking.

source.label: NASA — NASA’s InSight Mars Lander Gets a Power Boost

choices.label: Do nothing and wait for a dust devil to clean the panels
choices.outcome: Whirlwinds pass by the lander, recorded by its weather sensors. The panels stay dusty.

fact.title: Why not to rely on luck
fact.text: InSight’s weather sensors detected many passing whirlwinds, but none of them cleared any dust from its panels — unlike the luckier Spirit and Opportunity rovers.

source.label: NASA — NASA’s InSight Sees Power Levels Stabilize After Dust Storm

events.discuss: How could scientists tell the difference between a marsquake and a gust of wind?

events.title: Fight dust with dirt
telemetry: WIND: NW, UP TO 6 M/S AT NOON
events.text: Mars is near aphelion — the least sunlight of the year — and energy is falling. A scientist proposes something strange: use the arm’s scoop to pour sand into the wind so that bouncing sand grains knock the fine dust off a panel.

choices.label: Trickle sand near — not on — a panel at noon, the windiest time
choices.outcome: As sand blows across the panel, the power jumps: about 30 watt-hours more per sol. The team repeats it on 5 June. It buys a few extra weeks of science.

source.label: NASA — NASA’s InSight Mars Lander Gets a Power Boost

choices.label: Dump a full scoop straight onto the panel
choices.outcome: The sand mostly stays where it lands. The panel is now covered with sand as well as dust.

fact.title: Why the sand went next to the panel
fact.text: The idea was saltation: sand grains hop in the wind and strike the dust, carrying the finer particles away. The team deliberately trickled sand near, not directly on top of, the panels, at the windiest time of day.

source.label: NASA — NASA’s InSight Mars Lander Gets a Power Boost

choices.label: Order the Ingenuity helicopter to fly over and blow the dust off
choices.outcome: Request denied by the simulation: Ingenuity is in Jezero Crater, thousands of kilometres away, and could not reach InSight.

fact.title: A popular idea that could not work
fact.text: Members of the public suggested using Ingenuity’s blades to clean InSight’s panels. NASA explained that this was not an option.

source.label: NASA — NASA’s InSight Mars Lander Gets a Power Boost

events.discuss: Engineers used sand to clean a solar panel. What does this teach us about creative problem-solving with limited tools?

events.title: Regional dust storm
events.text: A large regional dust storm, first seen by the MARCI camera on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, darkens the sky. InSight has put itself into safe mode, suspending all but essential functions. The battery is low.

choices.label: Stay in safe mode, keep instruments off and wait for the sky to clear
choices.outcome: Contact is re-established on 10 January: power is low but steady. On 19 January InSight exits safe mode. By February the arrays produce almost as much as before the storm.

source.label: NASA — NASA’s InSight Sees Power Levels Stabilize After Dust Storm

choices.label: Turn SEIS back on — storms make great seismic data!

fact.title: Why safe mode exists
fact.text: In safe mode a spacecraft suspends all but essential functions to protect its batteries. Drained batteries are believed to have ended NASA’s Opportunity rover during the 2018 dust storms.

source.label: NASA — NASA’s InSight Sees Power Levels Stabilize After Dust Storm

events.discuss: Safe mode turns off almost everything. Why is doing less sometimes the safest choice?

events.title: One last picture
events.text: The arrays now produce roughly 500 watt-hours per sol — a tenth of what they made at landing. Moving the arm costs precious energy. The team must decide what the arm does last.

choices.label: Take a final selfie, then park the arm in its “retirement pose”
choices.outcome: InSight takes its final selfie on sol 1211 — the deck and panels caked in dust. In May the arm is parked for the last time, with its camera pointed at the seismometer.

source.label: NASA Science — InSight’s Final Selfie

choices.label: Keep scooping sand onto the panels every windy sol
choices.outcome: Each cleaning attempt now costs more energy than it returns.

fact.title: When a good trick stops working
fact.text: NASA noted that the sand-cleaning activities become increasingly difficult as available energy decreases — the arm itself needs power to move.

source.label: NASA — NASA’s InSight Sees Power Levels Stabilize After Dust Storm

events.discuss: Why did the team choose to take a final selfie instead of more science? Who was it for?

events.title: What gets the last watts?
events.text: There is only enough energy for one priority. Night is when winds are low and marsquakes are easiest to hear.

choices.label: Prioritise the seismometer, running at selected times such as night
choices.outcome: On 4 May 2022 — sol 1222 — SEIS records the largest quake ever detected on another planet, first estimated at magnitude 5 (later analysis: 4.7). Its waves keep ringing for hours.

source.label: NASA — NASA’s InSight Records Monster Quake on Mars

choices.label: Switch SEIS off now to stretch the mission’s lifetime
choices.outcome: The lander lives quietly — and on sol 1222 the biggest marsquake ever detected passes beneath a sleeping instrument.

fact.title: The quake you would have missed
fact.text: On sol 1222 InSight detected an estimated magnitude 5 marsquake, the largest observed on another planet. A peer-reviewed analysis later gave a moment magnitude of 4.7, with about five times the seismic moment of the previous largest event.

source.label: Kawamura et al. (2023), Geophysical Research Letters — S1222a

events.discuss: If you could keep only one instrument on, which one would you pick and why?

events.title: Listening for a heartbeat
events.text: After the summer, the seismometer was switched off. InSight has been sending occasional images and health data. On 15 December 2022 it talks to Earth one more time.

choices.label: Keep listening — declare the end only after two missed passes
choices.outcome: Two consecutive contact attempts fail. Engineers conclude the batteries are exhausted — “dead bus”. NASA retires InSight on 21 December 2022 but keeps listening, just in case.

source.label: NASA — NASA Retires InSight Mars Lander Mission After Years of Science

events.discuss: InSight is still on Mars. Should old landers be treated like museums, historic sites, or just hardware?

deadbus_storm.title: Dead bus in the storm
deadbus_storm.text: With the instruments drawing power under a darkened sky, the batteries drained. InSight fell silent during the January 2022 storm — almost a year earlier than the real mission.

real_end.title: Mission complete
real_end.text: You matched the real mission’s decisions. InSight worked for 1,440 sols — more than twice its one-Mars-year prime mission — and detected more than 1,300 marsquakes.

battery.title: Batteries exhausted
battery.text: The batteries dropped to zero. Without heaters, the electronics froze, and the lander stopped answering.

integrity.title: System failure
integrity.text: Too many risky operations: critical hardware failed and the lander could no longer be operated.

timeline: Landed in Elysium Planitia; solar arrays opened the same day.
Seismometer placed on the surface by the robotic arm.
Heat probe (“mole”) campaign; ended after it could not dig deeper.
Sand-trickling trick gave ~30 Wh per sol of extra power.
Safe mode during a regional dust storm.
Last contact. Mission declared over after two missed passes.

where.label: InSight lander, Elysium Planitia

coordSource.label: Golombek et al. (2020), Earth and Space Science — Location of the InSight lander

where.state: Silent on the surface since 15 December 2022, covered in dust. NASA continued to listen for a signal after retiring the mission.

inside.title: 2.4 million names
inside.text: Two silicon chips carrying about 2.4 million names submitted by the public were attached to the lander and remain on Mars.

source.label: NASA JPL — More Than 2.4 Million Names Are Going to Mars

inside.title: SEIS on the ground
inside.text: The French-built seismometer (CNES) still sits under its wind and thermal shield beside the lander.

source.label: NASA — InSight Records Monster Quake

inside.title: The mole
inside.text: DLR’s heat probe is buried just below the surface, its top 2–3 cm underground.

source.label: NASA — InSight’s ‘Mole’ Ends Its Journey
